title: What Happens When You Get Déjà Vu?
description:
Send this to the friend who always says 'I've been here before.'
An estimated 97% of people have had déjà vu (Cleveland Clinic). In a small St Andrews brain-scan study, the memory parts weren't the ones that lit up: frontal decision-making areas did, which researchers read as your brain fact-checking a false sense of familiarity (ScienceAlert; Memory, 2018; BBC Science Focus). In healthy people it usually happens a couple of times a year; seizures limited to the temporal lobe can also cause the feeling, so if it lasts longer than a few seconds or comes with confusion, loss of awareness or shaking, talk to a doctor (Cleveland Clinic).

structure_note: Brain-scan whodunit: two suspects (memory vs decision-maker), a crossed-wires mechanism, then a lab re-hook and the scan reveal. No diary, lineup, showdown, fuse, nerve map or two-paths. Beat 1: the hero frozen in a doorway of a new cafe, the same scene doubled behind him like a rerun film strip, x-ray cyan brain with pills 'A MEMORY' / 'B DECISION-MAKER'; a '97%' tag. Beat 2: inside the x-ray head, a 'MEMORY' wire and a 'NEW INFO' wire spark where they cross; the present moment gets stamped 'RERUN'. Relatable: hero walks into a new place, stops, squints. Re-hook: hard cut to a lab, hero in a scanner, word cards BED / PILLOW / DREAM fly past; a counter of 21 volunteer icons, 16 light up. Reveal: the scan glows at the FRONT of the brain, the memory area stays dark; pill B gets the check and a tiny magnifying-glass 'fact-checker' at the front. Safety line: calm card, a stopwatch passing 'a few seconds' and a doctor icon, no seizure visuals. Tease: a sweat drop, then cut back to the exact frame-1 doorway shot.
safety: Health-adjacent, curious-friend tone, no personal medical advice. Seizure link is in the description only, with Cleveland Clinic's own framing (temporal-lobe seizures can cause the feeling), preceded by its 'a couple times a year' for healthy people, no unsourced 'rare' claim; the voiced line uses Cleveland Clinic's own warning signs ('lasts longer than a few seconds', confusion) and points to a doctor, no scare framing. The answer reflects the researchers' interpretation (frontal decision areas checking), and the description says 'small study' and 'researchers read as'. Dropped as unsourced or not on reliable pages: rhinal cortex, '15-25 age peak', 'decreases with age' (not in Cleveland Clinic; Science Focus wording ambiguous), travel/dream/education link (true per Cleveland Clinic but cut for length).

engagement.guess: A memory vs B decision-maker: in the brain scan of lab-made déjà vu, which part lit up? (answer: B, decision-maker; ScienceAlert 2016 on O'Connor's St Andrews study: 'frontal areas of the brain associated with decision-making were activated' and 'the parts of the brain related to memory weren't the ones that lit up'; peer-reviewed as Urquhart et al. 2018, Memory: medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate. Option A is what most viewers expect, since déjà vu feels like a memory)
